This repository implements a Spring Boot-based REST API for managing book reviews, user accounts, and authentication. The application serves as a backend service for a book review platform, allowing users to register, log in, and interact with book data. The primary technology stack consists of Java, utilizing the Spring Boot framework version 4.0.6 as defined in the project dependencies. The codebase is predominantly written in Java, with supporting configuration files in XML and properties formats.

The architecture follows a standard Model-View-Controller (MVC) pattern with a distinct security layer. Incoming HTTP requests are first intercepted by a security middleware chain before reaching the business logic controllers. This chain includes a JWT filter for token validation and CORS configuration for cross-origin requests. Once authenticated, requests are routed to specific controllers which handle business logic and enforce role-based access control. Data persistence is managed through the Repository pattern, abstracting database interactions from the controller and security layers. The application follows a Model-View-Controller (MVC) architecture where HTTP requests are routed to specific controller methods that prepare data for server-side rendering. Data persistence and retrieval are abstracted behind the Repository Pattern, evidenced by the use of Spring Data interfaces such as `HomeServiceRepository`, `BookingRepository`, and `WorkerRepository` [C11, C13, C14]. These repositories are injected into controllers via constructor injection, ensuring loose coupling and testability. For example, `HomeController` receives `HomeServiceRepository` in its constructor [C12], while `WorkerController` injects `WorkerRepository`, `BookingRepository`, and an `EmailService` [C4]. This dependency injection pattern allows controllers to remain stateless and focused on request handling, delegating data access logic to the repository layer.

Authentication and state management are handled through the `HttpSession`, which acts as a server-side storage mechanism for user-specific data. This session-based approach contrasts with token-based authentication, relying on the server to maintain user state across requests.
